correctness.rationale: All 256 maps of a labeled four-state set are encoded bijectively by base-four integers; their full ordered square has 65,536 elements. BFS from the identity through composition with both generators enumerates precisely all word transformations, so vertex count is exact transition monoid size and shortest distance to any constant map is exact reset threshold. Independent Python computes monoid closure with tuple maps and reset depths using a separate 15-subset BFS; both agree cell-for-cell with the 179-row CSV. Independent symmetry conjugation checks produce exactly two 48-element orbits at reset depth nine, with monoid sizes 128 and 145. All computations were replayed from the delivered standalone files. The proof covers every pair with no inference to larger n.

value.rationale: The two independently natural invariants measure distinct structural resources: reset time and transformation-monoid diversity. The complete joint spectrum is not determined by known reset-threshold or monoid-size marginal results; it shows a sharp 31-element decline in maximum monoid size at the slowest attainable reset threshold, and distinguishes the 96 slowest automata into two explicit algebraic symmetry types. This exact natural small-state boundary is useful as a reference for structural conjectures about algebraic richness versus synchronization delay; it makes no unsupported large-state claim.
